notes.meaning: The Lord instructed Moses to tell Aaron how to set up the seven lamps on the golden lampstand. Aaron was to arrange them so they cast their light forward across the room toward the table of showbread. The tabernacle had no windows, so this light was needed for the priests to see and do their work.

Aaron obeyed the Lord's instruction right away and set the lamps to face forward. Even though tending lamps was a daily task, he did it with careful obedience. His prompt action showed respect for God in every detail of the sanctuary.

The lampstand was hammered out of a single piece of pure gold, from its solid base all the way to its flower-shaped cups. Moses did not follow his own ideas when making it. He followed the exact pattern God showed him on Mount Sinai.

God told Moses to separate the Levites from the rest of the Israelites and make them clean. They were chosen for holy service, but they received a simpler cleansing ritual than the priests had received. This helped remind them of their special duty to serve under the priests.

Moses had to sprinkle the Levites with special cleansing water to wash away ritual defilement, which was uncleanness that kept people from approaching God. The Levites then shaved all the hair from their bodies and washed their clothes. These outer washings pictured putting away sinful ways and serving God with pure hearts.

The Levites brought two young bulls along with a grain offering of fine flour mixed with olive oil. One bull was used for a burnt offering to show total dedication to God. The second bull was a sin offering to ask God's forgiveness for their wrongs.

Moses brought the Levites to the front of the tent of meeting and gathered the whole congregation of Israel. The entire nation took part in this event through their elders and tribal leaders. Everyone was able to see that God Himself had appointed these workers.

The leaders of Israel laid their hands upon the Levites before the Lord. By doing this, the people officially handed the Levites over to God in place of their own firstborn sons. The Levites became the living representatives of the whole nation in God's house.

Aaron presented the Levites before the Lord as a wave offering from the people of Israel. Since thousands of men could not be lifted and waved in the air, Aaron likely led them back and forth in front of the altar. This showed they were fully handed over to God and ready to do His work.

The Levites placed their hands on the heads of the two bulls before the animals were sacrificed. This action showed their sins were being symbolically transferred to the animals. An atonement—a sacrifice that covers sin and restores peace with God—had to be made before they could begin their sacred duties.

Moses placed the Levites before Aaron and the priests and offered them to the Lord. Once the Levites were given to God, God gave them back as helpers to the priests. This made it clear that they were to work under Aaron's direction.

These steps completely separated the Levites from the rest of the tribes so that they belonged only to God. They were excused from going to war and doing ordinary farming. Their whole life was now devoted to caring for the Lord's dwelling place.

Only after the Levites were washed and dedicated could they enter the courtyard to work. God required them to be cleansed before they could handle holy things. In the same way, God wants His servants to be clean in heart before doing His work.

The Lord declared that the Levites were entirely His own from among the Israelites. He accepted them in place of the firstborn son of every family. The Levites took over the holy duties that those firstborn sons would have performed.

God reminded the nation that every firstborn male belonged to Him because He spared them during the final plague in Egypt. Instead of taking the oldest son from each household, God took the entire tribe of Levi to serve Him. This trade freed the rest of the families while making sure God's house had full-time workers.

God gave the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons to serve the sanctuary on behalf of all the people. By standing guard around the holy tent, the Levites kept ordinary people from coming too close and bringing God's deadly judgment upon the camp. Their work protected the whole nation from harm.

Moses, Aaron, and the entire assembly carried out everything the Lord commanded concerning the Levites. The Levites purified themselves and washed their clothes, and Aaron presented them and made atonement for them. After that, they entered the sanctuary area and began their daily work under the priests.

The Lord told Moses that Levites were to begin their sanctuary service at twenty-five years old. Other passages mention age thirty for carrying the heaviest loads, showing that these first five years served as practical training. This rule made sure workers had the strength and maturity needed for sacred duties.

When a Levite reached fifty years of age, he was required to retire from heavy labor. God showed care for His workers by not forcing older men to lift and carry heavy tabernacle parts. This kept them from wearing out in old age.

Retired Levites were still allowed to assist their younger brothers with lighter duties around the tabernacle. They could stand guard at the gates, keep things in order, and share their wisdom. God relieved them of hard physical labor while still valuing their faithful service.
